title: Consonants: voicing, place, manner and nasality

blocks.main: **A consonant is made by narrowing or blocking the air somewhere in the mouth, and voicing is whether the vocal folds vibrate while you do it.** Say f as in fat and hold it, then say v as in vat and hold it. The lips and teeth stay in the same place for both, so the narrowing is the same. The difference is that the vocal folds vibrate for v and not for f, so v is **voiced** and f is **voiceless**.
sub: The same pair happens for th in thing and th in that, for s and z, and for sh and the j sound in beige. In each pair the place stays the same and only the voicing changes.
These sounds are **fricatives** (narrowing sounds), because the air squeezes through a narrow gap and makes a hissing noise.
blocks.end: So voicing is one dimension of a consonant, and it can change while everything else stays the same.

blocks.main: **Place of articulation is where in the mouth the narrowing happens, and the fricatives line up from the front of the mouth to the back.** The f and v are **labial** (made with the lower lip against the upper teeth). The two th sounds are **dental** (tongue tip at the teeth). The s and z are **alveolar** (tongue at the ridge just behind the upper teeth). The sh and the beige j sound are **postalveolar** (a little farther back than the ridge).
sub: In the MRI images the narrowing moves from the front of the mouth toward the back as you go across the table.
blocks.end: So place is the second dimension, and each fricative is one place combined with one voicing.

blocks.main: **A stop blocks the air completely somewhere in the mouth, and the stops come in groups of three by place.** The p, b and m are made at the lips (labial). The t, d and n are made at the alveolar ridge. The k, g and ng are made with the back of the tongue raised to the **velum** (the soft back part of the roof of the mouth).
sub: Within each group, p, t and k are voiceless and b, d and g are voiced, so p and b are a voicing pair with the same place, and so are t and d, and k and g.
The m, n and ng are **nasal stops**. The mouth is blocked in the same place as for b, d and g, but the velum is lowered, so the air comes out through the nose. They are all voiced.
blocks.end: So m and b share place and voicing and differ only in manner, because m lets the air out through the nose and b does not.

blocks.main: **Every English consonant is one combination of manner, voicing and place.** **Manner** is how the air is restricted, as a fricative (narrowed), an oral stop (blocked and then released through the mouth) or a nasal stop (blocked in the mouth and let out through the nose). **Voicing** is whether the vocal folds vibrate. **Place** is where the restriction is.
sub: Nasality can be counted as a fourth way to tell consonants apart, because it is whether the velum is lowered to let air through the nose.
A speaker knows this whole system without ever naming its parts, and that is part of what makes knowing a language a remarkable skill.
blocks.end: So to say how two consonants are similar and different, compare them one dimension at a time, manner, voicing and place.

questions.q: What is the similarity between s in sing and z in zing, and what is the difference?
questions.a: Both are fricatives made at the alveolar ridge, so they share manner and place. The difference is voicing. For z the vocal folds vibrate, so z is voiced. For s they do not, so s is voiceless.

questions.q: What is the similarity between t in tap and n in nap, and what is the difference?
questions.a: Both are stops made at the alveolar ridge, so they share place and a complete closure in the mouth. They differ in voicing and in nasality. The t is voiceless and oral, so the air is blocked and then released through the mouth. The n is voiced and nasal, so the velum is lowered and the air comes out through the nose.

questions.q: What are the different ways we distinguish the consonants at the beginning of fat, vat, sing and zing?
questions.a: All four are fricatives, so they are distinguished by place and by voicing. The f and v are labial, made with the lower lip against the upper teeth. The s and z are alveolar, made with the tongue at the ridge behind the upper teeth. The f and s are voiceless, and the v and z are voiced.

questions.q: Two vocal tract images are shown. In one the lips are closed and the velum is raised. In the other the lips are closed and the velum is lowered. Which is b and which is m?
questions.a: The b is the one with the velum raised, and the m is the one with the velum lowered. This is because both are made with the lips closed, so the lips do not tell them apart. For m the lowered velum opens the way to the nose, so the air comes out through the nose and m is nasal. For b the raised velum closes that way, so the air is blocked and then released through the mouth.

title: Vowels: tongue height, tongue frontness, and more than one frequency

blocks.main: **Vowels are told apart by where the tongue is, by its height and by its frontness.** Height is whether the tongue is high or low in the mouth. Frontness is whether the raised part of the tongue is toward the front or the back of the mouth.
sub: The vowel in dean is high and front. The vowel in dune is high and back. The vowel in Dan is low and front. The vowel in Don is low and back. The vowel in done is in the middle.
Moving the tongue changes where the air space above the vocal folds is narrow and where it is wide.
blocks.end: So each vowel is a different shape of the air space, made by a different tongue position.

blocks.main: **The air in a vowel does not vibrate at a single frequency, it vibrates at a combination of frequencies at once.** The illustrative /i/ model adds a slow vibration and a fast one, 1 cycle per second plus 4 cycles per second. The illustrative /a/ model adds 2 cycles per second plus 3 cycles per second. Both start at the same value, but inside each second they move very differently.
sub: Two air slices can be at different points at the same moment, so one can be compressed while the other is spread out.
The frequencies in the model are made slow on purpose so that the combination can be seen. Real vowel frequencies are hundreds of cycles per second.
blocks.end: So what makes /i/ sound different from /a/ is which frequencies are combined, not a single frequency.

blocks.main: **The tongue shape gives different parts of the air different mass and stiffness, and that is why one vowel contains several frequencies.** Where the tongue narrows the air space, that part of the air behaves differently from the part where there is more room. More mass makes a part vibrate more slowly, and more stiffness makes a part vibrate faster.
sub: So the vibrating air has a mix of lower, middle and higher frequencies, and the mix depends on the vowel.
To hear speech, the ear has to pick that mix apart and tell how strong each frequency is. That is how a listener tells scene from son.
blocks.end: So vowels connect the tongue, the physics of mass and stiffness, and hearing in one chain.

questions.q: What is the similarity and the difference between the vowels in Dan and Don?
questions.a: Both are low vowels, so the tongue is low in the mouth for both. The difference is that the vowel in Dan is a front vowel and the vowel in Don is a back vowel.

questions.q: What is the similarity and the difference between the vowels in dean and Dan?
questions.a: Both are front vowels, so the raised part of the tongue is toward the front of the mouth for both. The difference is height. The vowel in dean is high, and the vowel in Dan is low.

questions.q: Why does one vowel sound different from another, if both are just air vibrating in the vocal tract?
questions.a: The two vowels have different combinations of frequencies. This is because the tongue is in a different place for each vowel, so the air space has a different shape. A different shape gives different parts of the air different mass and stiffness, and different mass and stiffness mean different frequencies. So the air vibrates at a different mix of frequencies for each vowel, and the ear hears the difference in the mix.

title: Speech, the octopus, and what a dynamical system is

blocks.main: **A dynamical system is a set of elements with relationships between them, and their organized interaction produces behavior over time toward a goal.** To understand a behavior, name the elements, name the relationships among them, and name the goal their coordinated activity serves.
sub: A list of parts on its own does not explain the behavior. The relationships are what make the parts act together.
blocks.end: So the question to ask about any system is what the elements are, how they are related, and what they are for.

blocks.main: **An octopus keeping its den is a dynamical system made of eight arms, the ground and the fish it slaps at.** The arms interact with the ground and with the fish, so the environment is part of the system. A nervous system spread through the head and the body coordinates the arms.
sub: A study of 19 arm slaps found that the octopus combines simple movements, rotation (turning an arm) and translation (moving it along), one after another and at the same time, to make the complex slap.
The simple movements are planned ahead and then adjusted by feedback about where the moving fish is.
blocks.end: So a complex action is built from a few simple movements organized together, and the organization, not any one arm, explains the behavior.

blocks.ref: Lecture 03 · p5 · Lecture 01 · p2 · Lecture 02 · p3
blocks.main: **Speech is a dynamical system whose elements are the parts of the tongue, the lips, the velum, the larynx, the palate and the back wall of the throat.** The brain coordinates the relationships among these parts so that the shape of the vocal tract changes in the right way. The goal is to convey a thought.
sub: In the MRI videos the tongue reshapes while the openings in the mouth and throat change, and almost none of this can be seen from outside.
Listing the parts does not explain speaking. Their changing relationships produce the movement, the same way the arms and the ground together produce the octopus slap.
blocks.end: So speech, like the octopus, is explained by organized interaction, not by a list of parts.

blocks.main: **Very different systems can share the same organization, and that is why studying a simple one helps with a complicated one.** The heart, the pancreas, neurons and voluntary movements can all be studied as dynamical systems, with elements that are organs, cells or chemicals.
sub: Seeing the deep similarity between two systems that look different is creative reasoning, as opposed to treating things that merely look alike as the same.
blocks.end: So the same questions about elements, relationships and goals work for speech, for the body, and for AI.

more.main: **Children learn the extremely complex movements of speech with almost no teaching and no way to see their own speech organs.** By about age two to four they use a large vocabulary and most of the structure of adult language. Reading and writing, by contrast, develop around age six or seven and need a lot of instruction.
sub: **Articulatory phonetics** studies how the structures of the vocal tract move to make speech, and MRI makes those hidden movements visible.
Voice assistants and other speech technology copy parts of this human skill, which is why speech science and technology belong together.
more.end: So learning to speak is an impressive motor achievement, and speech technology is an attempt to build the same skill.

more.main: **Understanding how AI systems work matters because they have psychological, economic, social and environmental consequences, and possible benefits in medicine and engineering.** Knowing the arithmetic a system is built from does not by itself explain the complex behavior that comes out of it.
sub: That gap is the reason scientists, policy makers and lawyers need AI literacy, so that they can make useful decisions about these systems.
more.end: So the aim is to understand the systems well enough to judge their uses and their harms.

more.main: **Memorization and repetition handle familiar situations, and creative reasoning asks whether very different things share one structure.** Habits and specialized skills can make us treat similar things as identical and small differences as decisive. Creative reasoning instead asks questions and answers them, and looks for the hidden relationship.
sub: Diotima's ladder puts thought, focus, imagination, critical reading and creative writing above memorized answers.
more.end: So the recurring question is what two different systems have in common, and that is the skill to build.

more.main: **Artificial intelligence models psychological abilities, knowing, recognizing, attending, acting and learning, that animals including humans have.** The comparison is about how a skill can be organized, not about whether a machine has the same physical parts as an animal.
sub: Taylor's cloze procedure is an example of measuring knowledge through performance, by how well someone can restore a missing part of a message.
more.end: So each AI mechanism is matched with the human ability it models.

questions.q: What are the elements, the relationships and the goal of the speech system?
questions.a: The elements are the parts of the tongue, the lips, the velum, the larynx, the palate and the back wall of the throat. The relationships are the coordinated movements among those parts that change the shape of the vocal tract, which the brain organizes. The goal is to convey a thought.

questions.q: Why is a list of the speech organs not a complete explanation of speaking?
questions.a: A list of the parts leaves out the relationships between them, and the relationships are what produce the behavior. Speaking happens because the tongue, lips, velum and larynx move together in an organized way toward the goal of conveying a thought. So the explanation has to say how the parts interact, not just what they are.

questions.q: What makes the octopus arm slap a dynamical system, and what does it have in common with speech?
questions.a: The arm slap has elements, the eight arms, the ground and the fish, that interact through relationships coordinated by the nervous system, toward the goal of keeping the den. Speech has the same organization, with the tongue, lips, velum and larynx as elements, coordinated by the brain, toward the goal of conveying a thought. In both, the behavior comes from the organized interaction of the parts, not from any one part on its own.

title: Closure, the cloze task and how GPT learns

blocks.main: **Closure is the tendency to complete a familiar pattern that is unfinished.** A broken circle is seen as a whole circle, because familiarity with the shape lets the mind close the gap. Three black disks with wedges cut out are seen as a triangle, even though no triangle is drawn.
sub: Cloze is pronounced like close and is named after closure. It takes the same idea from shapes to language. The reader uses the words that remain to fill in the word that is missing.
blocks.end: So closure means filling in what is missing from what is already known.

blocks.main: **The cloze procedure deletes words from a message and measures how well people can restore them.** In "Chickens cackle and ___ quack," the missing word is ducks. Each correct restoration counts as one cloze unit.
sub: Filling the gap takes more than knowing one word. It takes the meanings of the words, the way chickens goes with cackle and ducks with quack, and the parallel shape of the sentence.
Wilson Taylor introduced the procedure in 1953 as a way to measure how readable a text is.
blocks.end: So knowledge can be tested through the ability to complete a sequence, and that is how a language model shows what it knows.

blocks.main: **GPT learns by doing the cloze task billions of times.** It takes a sentence, hides part of it, and makes the network guess the missing word. If the guess is wrong, the weights are changed a little. After billions of completions, the weights hold the knowledge of the language.
sub: Completing a sequence is predicting what fits the context, and people do the same thing when they expect what comes next.
Whether this counts as knowledge is a debate. One view is that the system's knowledge is not so different from ours, and a skeptical view, associated with Yann LeCun, says it is.
blocks.end: So closure is the principle, the cloze task is the method, and prediction is what the system learns to do.

questions.q: A sentence has a word hidden, and a language model guesses the wrong word. What happens next, and why does this count as learning?
questions.a: The wrong guess gets compared with the real missing word, and the difference is the mistake. The weights are then changed a little in the direction that would have made the right word more likely. This counts as learning because the weights hold the knowledge, so changing them changes what the network knows. After billions of these corrections the guesses become right.

questions.q: What do a broken circle and the sentence Chickens cackle and ___ quack have in common?
questions.a: In both, something is missing and the mind fills it in from what is already there. The circle is completed from familiarity with its shape, and the sentence is completed with ducks from the meanings of the other words and the parallel pattern of the sentence. Both are closure, which is completing a familiar but unfinished pattern.

title: What a neural network outputs: a probability distribution and a decision

blocks.main: **A neural network takes in a signal as a list of numbers and gives out a probability distribution over the possible identities.** A face image can be 48 million pixel numbers, and the question is which of 1000 people it is. A speech wave is a list of pressure numbers, and the question is which of 25 sounds it is.
sub: For five vowels in the order read, rad, rude, Rud, rod, the output [0.2, 0.2, 0.4, 0.2, 0] gives 20 percent to read, 20 percent to rad, 40 percent to rude, 20 percent to Rud and 0 to rod.
The decision is the category with the largest number, so here the decision is rude.
blocks.end: So the output is not one answer but a set of probabilities, and the decision is the biggest one.

blocks.main: **A probability distribution is a list where every number is between 0 and 1 and all the numbers add up to 1.** A list that adds up to 0, or to 1.5, is not a distribution, and neither is a list with a negative number in it.
sub: The list only means something together with the agreed order of the categories. The same numbers in a different order would be a different decision.
For example, [.4, 0, .5, .2] is not a good output for four categories, because the numbers add up to 1.1.
blocks.end: So to check an output, check that each number is between 0 and 1 and that the total is exactly 1.

blocks.main: **The true answer is given to the network as a distribution with all of the probability on the correct category.** If the correct vowel is Rud, the fourth of five, the target is [0, 0, 0, 1, 0]. The network's own output might be [0.4, 0.1, 0.2, 0.2, 0.1], which puts the most probability on read.
sub: Comparing the output with the target gives the error, which is also called the loss. Training changes the weights to make that error smaller.
The input numbers can be positive or negative and are not probabilities. Only the output is a probability distribution.
blocks.end: So the target is the same kind of list as the output, with a 1 in the right place and 0 everywhere else.

blocks.main: **For a language model the categories are the possible next words, so the output is a probability for each word.** Each input word is a vector (a list of numbers), for example 1,024 numbers per word. The model uses the whole sequence, chickens, cackle, and, ducks, to predict the next word.
sub: The output is another vector, for example 10,000 numbers, one for each possible next word such as a, cat, quack and Zulu. The number for quack should be the biggest.
blocks.end: So a language model's decision is the next word with the highest probability.

questions.q: Is [.2, .3, .5] a good output of a neural network with three categories? Is [.5, .5, .5]?
questions.a: The first one is good, because each number is between 0 and 1 and they add up to 1. The second one is not good, because the numbers add up to 1.5. A probability distribution has to add up to exactly 1.

questions.q: A network's output is [.1, .6, .2, .1] and the true category is the third one. Write the true answer as a probability distribution. Is the network's decision right?
questions.a: The true answer is [0, 0, 1, 0], with all the probability on the third category. The network's decision is wrong, because its biggest number, .6, is in the second position, so it decided on the second category. The gap between its output and the target is the error that training uses to fix the weights.

title: Knowledge in the weights: inner products and forward propagation

blocks.main: **A network's knowledge is stored in its weights, which are the numbers that determine how the inputs get turned into output probabilities.** The input words are vectors called x's, and the weights are called w's. The computation that combines them uses only adding, subtracting, multiplying and dividing, but a very large interconnected system of these operations can do something complex.
sub: Some large AI systems have trillions of weights. The brain stores the same kind of knowledge in its synapses (the connections between neurons), about 150 trillion of them.
Changing the weights changes which next words get high or low probability for the same input.
blocks.end: So learning means changing the weights, because that is where the knowledge is.

blocks.main: **Each neuron multiplies every incoming activation by its own weight and adds the products, and that sum is the inner product.** An **activation** is the number coming in from a neuron in the layer before. A **weight** is the number on one connection, and it can be positive or negative.
sub: With inputs of minus 1, 1 and 3 and weights of minus 2, 3 and 1, the products are 2, 3 and 3, and the sum is 8.
A positive weight keeps the sign of the input, and a negative weight changes it. For example, an input of 3 with a weight of 2 gives 6, and the same input with a weight of minus 2 gives minus 6.
The inner product is also called the dot product or the scalar product. It is the core calculation of all neural networks.
blocks.end: So a neuron with 5 inputs has 5 weights, and its activation is w1 times x1 plus w2 times x2 and so on up to w5 times x5.

blocks.main: **The inner product is a way of comparing two lists of numbers, so the weights act as templates that the input is matched against.** With an input of [minus 1, 3, minus 2], the template [minus 2, 0, 3] gives 2 plus 0 minus 6, which is minus 4. The template [minus 2, 2, minus 1] gives 2 plus 6 plus 2, which is 10.
sub: A big positive inner product means a strong match, and a value near zero means little match, so the second template matches better.
In the templatic theory of face perception, the brain compares an incoming face with stored templates, and the most similar template decides who it is. The weights play the part of the templates.
blocks.end: So before learning the templates are random and the matches are poor, and training makes the templates useful.

blocks.main: **Forward propagation is the calculation that runs from the input layer to the output layer using the current weights.** A network with 5 inputs, hidden layers of 3, 4 and 3 neurons, and 7 outputs has every neuron connected to every neuron in the next layer, which is 60 connections, each with its own weight.
sub: Each neuron in the first hidden layer takes the inner product of the 5 inputs with its 5 weights. Those 3 activations become the inputs to the next layer, which does the same, and so on through the layers.

With inputs [2, 1, 3, 4, 2] and weights [2, minus 1, 1, 3, minus 2], the middle hidden neuron gets 4 minus 1 plus 3 plus 12 minus 4, which is 14. With inputs [minus 2, 1, 3, minus 4, 2] and weights [3, minus 2, 1, 2, 5] the sum is minus 6 minus 2 plus 3 minus 8 plus 10, which is minus 3. Hidden activations can be negative.
The last layer turns its numbers into a probability distribution, for example [0.05, 0.10, 0.20, 0.30, 0.15, 0.12, 0.08], and the fourth category, at 0.30, is the decision.
blocks.end: So the output depends on the inputs and on every weight along the way, and the signs matter at every step.

blocks.ref: Lecture 09 · p14 · Lecture 09 · p16 · Lecture 10 · p5
blocks.main: **Perception works in stages, and a network copies that by turning each layer's output into the next layer's input.** In the visual system, areas V1, V2, V3 and V4 and the areas after them each transform the information and pass it on, with connections running forward and back.
sub: **Inference** is using the current weights to compute an output for an input. **Learning** is changing the weights. A training step has to run inference first, to get the output it will compare with the correct answer, so inference is part of learning.
Like Euler's method, a network builds a complex result out of many repeated simple calculations.
blocks.end: So a hierarchy of template comparisons, layer after layer, is what a neural network is.

more.main: **A speech recognizer that receives a [z] sound wave has to compare it with what it has learned, and two ideas from animal perception organize that comparison.** Template matching compares the input with stored patterns. Hierarchical processing turns the input into a new representation and then transforms that again, stage after stage.
sub: A neural network combines both, by comparing numerical patterns at several levels one after another.
more.end: So recognition is matching plus stages.

more.main: **Neural network models translate ideas about brain activity into arithmetic.** The line runs from McCulloch and Pitts in 1943, through Rosenblatt's perceptrons in 1962, to the Parallel Distributed Processing books of 1986. Each one tries to copy some part of what neurons do with formal operations.
sub: One view says AI and human thinking are fundamentally different, because brain chemistry is not arithmetic. The other view treats AI as a long attempt to use arithmetic to copy parts of brain activity. This comparison is outside the exam.
more.end: So the arithmetic is a model of the brain, not a claim that the two are made of the same stuff.

questions.q: A neuron in layer 3 is connected to 7 neurons in layer 2. How many weights does it have, and how is its activation written?
questions.a: It has 7 weights, one on each incoming connection. Its activation is w1 times x1 plus w2 times x2 and so on up to w7 times x7, where the x's are the 7 activations coming in and the w's are the 7 weights. Each input is multiplied by its own weight and the products are added.

questions.q: A neuron has inputs 2, minus 1 and 3 with weights 1, 4 and minus 2. What is its activation, and what is this calculation called?
questions.a: Its activation is minus 8. This is because the products are 2 times 1, which is 2, then minus 1 times 4, which is minus 4, then 3 times minus 2, which is minus 6, and 2 minus 4 minus 6 is minus 8. The calculation is the inner product, which multiplies each input by its weight and adds the results.

questions.q: What is the difference between inference and learning in a neural network?
questions.a: Inference uses the weights the network has now to compute an output for an input. Learning changes the weights. The two are linked, because a learning step first runs inference to get the current output, then compares it with the correct answer, then changes the weights to shrink the difference. So inference is part of every learning step, but only the weight change is learning.

questions.q: Why can an input of 3 end up pushing a neuron's activation down?
questions.a: It pushes the activation down when its weight is negative. This is because the input is multiplied by its weight, so 3 times a negative weight such as minus 2 gives minus 6, which lowers the sum. The sign of the weight decides whether an input adds to the activation or subtracts from it.
